vignette:
Arjun Patel had worked for an international aid organization in his early thirties, sent into a war zone to help with relief coordination after bombardments had torn apart a neighborhood of apartments, a clinic, and the small cemetery behind the mosque. One afternoon, while he was moving between damaged buildings with local staff, a shelling strike ignited fuel and debris nearby. The smoke came fast and thick, carrying the sharp, acrid smell of fire that seemed to cling to his clothes and hair. In the chaos, people were shouting, some with anger and some with grief, and Arjun found himself trying to shepherd frightened families toward cover while also hearing the cries from the cemetery side where several graves had been disturbed. He remembers pieces of that day in fragments: the blast, the smell, a body on the ground, someone yelling at him, his own hands shaking in front of his face. Even now, when he tries to tell the story, the sequence slips apart; he cannot put the memories in the right order, and that confusion only deepens his sense that something unforgivable happened while he stood there.

Since returning home, Arjun has found that the smell of smoke or fire can pull him back in an instant. A passing car with a burnt engine, food left too long on the stove, even incense near a temple during a family visit can make his chest tighten and his mind go blank with the feeling that he is back in that ruined street. When that happens he covers his face with his hands without thinking, as if hiding from what he has remembered, and he gets away from the source of the smell as quickly as possible. The cues do more than startle him; they set off a surge of danger that feels immediate and real, and at the same time the smell or sight opens the memory of that afternoon before he can steady himself. In those moments he is flooded with the thought that if smoke can still find him anywhere, then he is never really out of reach of what happened. He avoids the site of the event whenever work or travel might bring him near that district, and he steers clear of funerals, cemeteries, or any grief-related gathering because the sight of mourning families and disturbed earth brings the day rushing back. He has also begun avoiding situations that might make him feel happy or hopeful, turning down invitations and keeping celebrations at arm's length, as though allowing himself any relief would be reckless. At home in his role as a tax consultant, he has become more withdrawn in the office, declining lunch outings and leaving earlier so he does not have to linger in situations that feel emotionally exposed. Staying away feels like the only sensible response to him, because once the trigger has landed he experiences the world as dangerous all over again. In that state even ordinary days at the office feel like a place where something could go wrong, so he keeps himself small and moves quickly through the workday.

Arjun had come to believe that the world no longer worked according to any rules he could trust. What frightened him most was not only what happened there, but what it seemed to mean about him: he should have protected others and failed. That belief rose up whenever he remembered the people he could not save, and the shame felt physical, as if his body returned to the same crouched position it had taken behind a wall while the shelling continued. The more he recalls that day, the more certain he becomes that he is set apart from other people, carrying something damaged and dishonorable that they would not understand. That conviction made the smallest cues feel loaded for him: a thin ribbon of smoke from a kitchen vent, a funeral notice, even an angry tone across a room could snag his attention and seem to announce danger before anyone else in the room had noticed anything at all. Because he already believed the world had gone wrong and that his own judgement could not be trusted, ordinary reminders did not stay ordinary for long; they became proof that the threat was still near. Those thoughts do not stay abstract; they shape where he goes and what he allows himself to feel. If he notices smoke, hears about a funeral, or senses anger in another person's voice-even when it is calm-he pulls back, covers his face, and keeps away, as if distance can keep him from being overwhelmed again. Once he had decided that he was unsafe to himself and inadequate to others, almost any reminder could confirm it - a whiff of smoke, a raised voice, a mention of the dead. The more certain he became that he had failed and could not trust his own judgement, the more every cue seemed to carry a warning that something terrible was about to happen.

Yet the distance has not brought relief. By avoiding the event site and anything that resembles the loss, Arjun has found himself thinking about it more, not less; the memories arrive with less warning, and when they do, the shame lands harder. He notices his body tensing in the middle of ordinary tasks, and the same sense of helplessness returns with it. The more he hides and retreats, the more isolated and set apart he feels, which only confirms his belief that something about him has been permanently altered. That persistent sense of danger kept pulling the day back toward him at night, as if his mind could not afford to let the memory sit untouched while he stayed on alert. On the evenings when the house felt least safe, the scene returned most vividly, not because he chose it, but because the threat still felt unfinished. At night this is worst: the house feels less safe than in daylight, and ordinary sounds-a door closing, a bicycle bell outside, his wife moving in the kitchen-make him jump. He lies awake scanning for danger, his attention broken and scattered, and the fatigue bleeds into his work, where concentration has become difficult enough that he rereads the same figures over and over. Not speaking about it and not going back there has left the memory undisturbed, so it comes back vivid and intact, often at the very moments he is trying hardest not to think about it. Each return of the image seems to prove his worst fear about himself, that there is something permanently damaged in him, and that proof keeps his mind fixed on danger long after the original event.

His wife has tried to pull him into family dinners and weekend plans, but he often refuses, especially if they are meant to be cheerful. He is afraid that if he lets himself feel hopeful, it will only make the fall worse. The avoidance has narrowed his life, and with each retreat his belief that he failed to protect others and cannot trust the world becomes more solid. He finally sought help after a night when the smell of smoke from a neighbor's cooking fire sent him into a panic, he spent hours awake listening for sounds outside, and the next morning he made an error at work because he could not concentrate. Arjun came in hoping to stop feeling hunted by reminders, and fearing that if nothing changes he will remain trapped in the shame of that day, unable to be present with his wife, his work, or any future that might still be possible. The more he pulled away from dinners, celebrations, and ordinary closeness, the more his life became a map of places and situations he could no longer tolerate. By refusing to talk about it and by keeping anything that might remind him at a distance, he had never really put the memory anywhere; it stayed in him, undisturbed and intact, and when it surfaced it came back with the same force it had carried in the first place. The effort of holding it away seemed to have kept it close. Having never stayed long enough to discover that those moments were safe, he experienced the danger as ongoing, and that made even a normal evening at home feel like a test he might fail.

What frightened him most was not only what happened there, but what it seemed to mean about him: he should have protected others and failed. That belief rose up whenever he remembered the people he could not save, and the shame felt physical, as if his body returned to the same crouched position it had taken behind a wall while the shelling continued. The more he recalls that day, the more certain he becomes that he is set apart from other people, carrying something damaged and dishonorable that they would not understand. That conviction made the smallest cues feel loaded for him: a thin ribbon of smoke from a kitchen vent, a funeral notice, even an angry tone across a room could snag his attention and seem to announce danger before anyone else in the room had noticed anything at all. Because he already believed the world had gone wrong and that his own judgement could not be trusted, ordinary reminders did not stay ordinary for long; they became proof that the threat was still near. Those thoughts do not stay abstract; they shape where he goes and what he allows himself to feel. If he notices smoke, hears about a funeral, or senses anger in another person’s voice—even when it is calm—he pulls back, covers his face, and keeps away, as if distance can keep him from being overwhelmed again. Once he had decided that he was unsafe to himself and inadequate to others, almost any reminder could confirm it — a whiff of smoke, a raised voice, a mention of the dead. The more certain he became that he had failed and could not trust his own judgement, the more every cue seemed to carry a warning that something terrible was about to happen.

Yet the distance has not brought relief. By avoiding the event site and anything that resembles the loss, Arjun has found himself thinking about it more, not less; the memories arrive with less warning, and when they do, the shame lands harder. He notices his body tensing in the middle of ordinary tasks, and the same sense of helplessness returns with it. The more he hides and retreats, the more isolated and set apart he feels, which only confirms his belief that something about him has been permanently altered. That persistent sense of danger kept pulling the day back toward him at night, as if his mind could not afford to let the memory sit untouched while he stayed on alert. On the evenings when the house felt least safe, the scene returned most vividly, not because he chose it, but because the threat still felt unfinished. At night this is worst: the house feels less safe than in daylight, and ordinary sounds—a door closing, a bicycle bell outside, his wife moving in the kitchen—make him jump. He lies awake scanning for danger, his attention broken and scattered, and the fatigue bleeds into his work, where concentration has become difficult enough that he rereads the same figures over and over. Not speaking about it and not going back there has left the memory undisturbed, so it comes back vivid and intact, often at the very moments he is trying hardest not to think about it. Each return of the image seems to prove his worst fear about himself, that there is something permanently damaged in him, and that proof keeps his mind fixed on danger long after the original event.

His wife has tried to pull him into family dinners and weekend plans, but he often refuses, especially if they are meant to be cheerful. He is afraid that if he lets himself feel hopeful, it will only make the fall worse. The avoidance has narrowed his life, and with each retreat his belief that he failed to protect others and cannot trust the world becomes more solid. He finally sought help after a night when the smell of smoke from a neighbor’s cooking fire sent him into a panic, he spent hours awake listening for sounds outside, and the next morning he made an error at work because he could not concentrate. Arjun came in hoping to stop feeling hunted by reminders, and fearing that if nothing changes he will remain trapped in the shame of that day, unable to be present with his wife, his work, or any future that might still be possible. The more he pulled away from dinners, celebrations, and ordinary closeness, the more his life became a map of places and situations he could no longer tolerate. By refusing to talk about it and by keeping anything that might remind him at a distance, he had never really put the memory anywhere; it stayed in him, undisturbed and intact, and when it surfaced it came back with the same force it had carried in the first place. The effort of holding it away seemed to have kept it close. Having never stayed long enough to discover that those moments were safe, he experienced the danger as ongoing, and that made even a normal evening at home feel like a test he might fail.
